lead: The first law gives energy changes; the second law gives entropy changes. The four fundamental property relations combine both laws into exact differentials for internal energy U, enthalpy H, Helmholtz free energy A and Gibbs free energy G. Each differential names the natural variables of one potential and lets you read derivatives directly from its coefficients. Chemical engineers use these relations to compute property changes from pressure–volume–temperature data, design compressors and heat exchangers, and build the property packages inside process simulators.
prereq: You need Unit 1 (first law for closed systems), Unit 2 (equations of state) and Unit 3 (entropy); free energies are defined in 4.1.

sections.h3: From two laws to four exact differentials

blocks.text: Take a closed, simple compressible system: no chemical reaction, no shaft work, negligible kinetic and potential energy. For a reversible path the system pressure equals the external pressure P and the system temperature equals the bath temperature T. The first law is dU = δQ − δW. The second law for a reversible path gives δQ = T dS. The only work is P dV, so δW = P dV. Therefore dU = T dS − P dV.
Define the other potentials by Legendre transforms: H = U + PV, A = U − TS, and G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Differentiate each definition and substitute dU. The P dV and T dS terms cancel in pairs.
dU = T dS − P dV; dH = T dS + V dP; dA = −S dT − P dV; dG = −S dT + V dP
blocks.where: U is internal energy (J), H enthalpy (J), A Helmholtz free energy (J), G Gibbs free energy (J). T is temperature (K), S entropy (J/K), P pressure (Pa), V volume (m³).

blocks.text: Each left side is an exact differential; each right side contains only the natural variables of that potential. Some syllabi call these the thermodynamic property relations.

An exact differential dz = M dx + N dy has M = (∂z/∂x)<sub>y</sub> and N = (∂z/∂y)<sub>x</sub>. Compare this with each relation. The comparison identifies the natural variables and the coefficient identities.

The subscript on each derivative says what is held constant. For example, (∂U/∂S)<sub>V</sub> = T means entropy changes at fixed volume; (∂U/∂V)<sub>S</sub> = −P means volume changes at fixed entropy. A partial derivative is not a simple fraction: (∂U/∂S)<sub>V</sub> is not dU divided by dS in the ordinary sense.
Equality of mixed second derivatives of these potentials gives the Maxwell relations (see 4.3). That step replaces entropy derivatives by measurable pressure, volume and temperature derivatives.

sections.h3: Integrating the relations for property changes

blocks.text: Because U, H, A and G are state functions, integrate along any convenient reversible path between the same two states. Choose a path that matches the natural variables. At constant T, dA = −P dV and dG = V dP; at constant S, dU = −P dV and dH = V dP.

For an ideal gas, U and H depend only on T. Then dU = C<sub>V</sub> dT and dH = C<sub>P</sub> dT, where C<sub>V</sub> is heat capacity at constant volume (J/K) and C<sub>P</sub> is heat capacity at constant pressure (J/K). Entropy follows from dS = C<sub>V</sub> dT/T + R dV/V, or dS = C<sub>P</sub> dT/T − R dP/P, with R the gas constant (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). For a real gas, insert its equation of state.

At constant temperature, a useful identity for real gases is (∂U/∂V)T = T(∂P/∂T)V − P. It follows by dividing dU = T dS − P dV by dV at fixed T and using the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)T = (∂P/∂T)V from 4.3. It turns a hard entropy derivative into a measurable PVT derivative.

figure.caption: Adding PV to U gives H; subtracting TS gives A; subtracting TS from H gives G. Each box carries its exact differential.

spec.aria: U is the root; adding PV gives H, subtracting TS gives A, and subtracting TS from H gives G, with each potential showing its differential.

examples.question: A van der Waals gas obeys P = RT/(V − b) − a/V², with a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻². At T = 300 K and V = 0.200 m³ mol⁻¹, calculate (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub>.
steps: Start from the coefficient identity (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P.
Differentiate P with respect to T at fixed V. The term RT/(V − b) gives R/(V − b); the term −a/V² has no T, so its derivative is zero.
Subtract P: T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P = RT/(V − b) − [RT/(V − b) − a/V²] = a/V².
Insert a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻² and V = 0.200 m³ mol⁻¹. V² = 0.0400 m⁶ mol⁻².
a/V² = 0.364/0.0400 = 9.1 Pa. The constants b and T cancel, so the result does not depend on their values here.
The derivative is positive: at fixed T, U rises as V rises for this van der Waals gas.
examples.check:
a = 0.364
V = 0.200
result = a / V**2
print(round(result, 1))

traps: Mixing up natural variables: U is natural in (S,V), not (T,V). H is natural in (S,P), not (T,P).
Using the wrong sign for P dV: dU = T dS − P dV and dA = −S dT − P dV both carry a minus sign on P dV.
Treating a partial derivative as a simple fraction: (∂U/∂V)<sub>S</sub> cannot be cancelled with dV.
Using dG = −S dT + V dP for a mixture with changing composition. The full relation then needs chemical potential terms (Unit 5).
Confusing (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> with (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub>; they are different derivatives and different identities.

quiz.q: Write dU for a reversible closed simple compressible system. Define each symbol.
quiz.a: dU = T dS − P dV; U internal energy (J), T temperature (K), S entropy (J/K), P pressure (Pa), V volume (m³).

quiz.q: Give the natural variables of H and G.
Why is H = U + PV a Legendre transform, and what variable does it change?
quiz.a: It replaces V by P as an independent variable. dH = dU + P dV + V dP cancels −P dV, giving dH = T dS + V dP.

quiz.q: From dA = −S dT − P dV, write (∂A/∂T)<sub>V</sub> and (∂A/∂V)<sub>T</sub>.
For an ideal gas, show (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = 0 using the coefficient identity.
quiz.a: P = RT/V; (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = R/V. Then T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P = RT/V − P = 0. So U depends only on T.

quiz.q: Explain why (∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> is negative for a stable phase.
quiz.a: dG = −S dT + V dP, so (∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −S. Entropy S is positive for a stable phase at ordinary T, so G falls as T rises at fixed P.

quiz.q: For a van der Waals gas with a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻² and V = 0.100 m³ mol⁻¹, compute (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store property packages built on these exact differentials. Departure functions integrate the same relations from zero pressure to the real pressure; that is the subject of 4.4. The Joule–Thomson coefficient and speed of sound also come from these derivatives. Search next for 'fundamental equation of thermodynamics', 'Maxwell relations' and 'departure functions'.
